_comment: Guided tour for the non-burst IRF/background extractor. Targets are the AutoForm view-spec entries of irf_bg.view.json. The centrepiece is the documented two-fold lifetime bias a naive baseline subtraction causes -- that is the reason this tool exists, so the tour says so with the numbers. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: The measurement you already paid for
steps.text:
Most of a confocal acquisition contains no molecule in the focus. Those non-burst periods are usually discarded — but they are a scatter and background measurement sitting in the file you already have.

One pass over them gives, per detector, both a background rate and an IRF. No scatter cuvette, no buffer-only run, and no chance the IRF was measured under different conditions than the data. Seven steps.

steps.title: Two things, and they separate in micro-time
steps.text:
Dark counts and after-pulses are uncorrelated with the laser, so they are flat across the micro-time axis. That floor is the background rate.

Scattered excitation is instantaneous, so it is a sharp prompt peak — and the shape of that peak is the instrument response.

Define the detectors first: each channel has its own response, and a shared IRF becomes a systematic lifetime shift that differs between channels — indistinguishable from a real difference between the dyes.

steps.title: The same files the bursts came from
steps.text: The non-burst photons are, by definition, everything the burst search did not select. So this reads the same raw files and inverts the burst mask rather than searching again.

steps.title: What counts as a burst to be excluded
steps.text:
These settings define the mask that is inverted. Being generous here is the safe direction: a burst photon wrongly left in the non-burst stream adds fluorescence to what is supposed to be pure scatter, and that is the failure the next step is about.

Excluding a little too much costs only statistics.

steps.title: Extract
steps.text: For each detector: fit the interphoton-time tail for the background rate, histogram the non-burst micro-times, subtract the flat dark-count floor, and fit the prompt.

steps.title: Why there is a Gaussian on top of your data
steps.text:
A baseline-subtracted non-burst histogram is not an IRF. The non-burst periods still hold dim and passing molecules, so the prompt rides on a slow fluorescent tail, and a flat subtraction removes the dark counts while leaving that decay behind.

Convolving a lifetime model with such an "IRF" biases the result roughly two-fold short — a genuine 2.2 ns decay came back at ~1.1 ns on real data.

So the prompt is fitted with a Gaussian, precisely because a Gaussian cannot represent a slow tail: least squares locks onto the sharp scatter peak and leaves the artefact behind. The width comes from the rising edge only — the falling side is the decay, not the instrument.

steps.title: Four checks before you fit with these
steps.text:
1. Does the prompt look like a prompt? One sharp peak. Structure or a shoulder means the mask is letting fluorescence through — go back and exclude more.
2. Does the fitted Gaussian sit on the rising edge? If it sits late, the tail has captured it.
3. Is the background rate plausible? Hundreds of Hz to a few kHz per detector; much more is stray light.
4. Does a known sample return its known lifetime? The only end-to-end check that matters — and the one that caught the two-fold bias above.

The ? button has the long version.
